warnings: Lesson is long at 4741 words; consider tightening for reading flow.
Quiz language appears sparse; make assessment prompts explicit.

improvement_notes: The lesson is technically strong but substantially overlong for a single foundational dynamics class. Several ideas recur in the opening, The Big Idea, Core Concept, What Should Happen?, and Common Mistakes sections. Consolidate repeated explanations of net force, mass, constant velocity, and lateral force to reduce cognitive load.

Add a short explicit section distinguishing the selected system boundary from alternative boundaries. For example, if analyzing the toolbox alone, gripper contact becomes external; if analyzing the complete rover-plus-toolbox system, it is internal. The current explanation implies this correctly but requires careful reading.

The mathematical and numerical-method depth is excellent, but the full Python listing is disproportionately large relative to the conceptual lesson. Consider moving edge-case verification and the non-integer-duration helper into an advanced appendix or expandable enrichment section.
The beginner path would benefit from a small worked prediction table before the code, showing mass, net force, acceleration, final velocity, and analytic position for both rover cases.

The braking extension is appropriately labeled as simulation-only, but physical testing guidance should also require instructor supervision, a tested emergency stop, a bounded test area, and a method for disabling motion remotely. 'Clear area at low speed' is helpful but not a complete robotics test protocol.

The lesson introduces rotational dynamics, yaw rate, torque, payload geometry, and tipping responsibly, but these connections could be visually separated as optional context so beginners do not confuse them with the one-dimensional model.

The phrase 'the force required to start, stop, or turn' is broadly understandable but should note that turning demand depends on both translational force and rotational dynamics, especially for differential-drive robots.

The generated visual plan is strong, but the lesson would be even more grounded by adding a real photograph showing a mobile robot carrying an offset payload, with a caption directing attention to wheel contact, center of mass, and tipping-relevant geometry.

The vocabulary section is useful, though 'translational dynamics' could be phrased more precisely as the study of translational motion under forces, rather than only forces that change position or velocity.

Consider adding one brief formative question immediately after the free-body-diagram explanation asking learners to redraw the diagram for the toolbox alone. This would test system-boundary transfer rather than recognition.
